title: Nature's prescription
hook: as doctors prescribe cold baths, nature prescribes illness or loss; take it like medicine (Meditations 5.8)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Marcus, and what is wholly yours: sincerity, dignity, endurance. Your line was what is mine.

Physical therapy hurts. The stretch you're told to hold for thirty seconds feels like three minutes. The exercise for your knee is boring and sore. And yet people do it, more or less cheerfully, because someone they trust wrote it down and said: this will help. You don't argue with a prescription the way you argue with bad luck. Marcus Aurelius noticed that difference, and in book five, entry eight, he tried to move the hard things in his life from one column to the other.
screen: `PHYSICAL THERAPY HURTS.` → `YOU DON'T ARGUE WITH A PRESCRIPTION.` → `NATURE'S PRESCRIPTION.`

segments.voice: People say, Marcus writes, Asclepius prescribed this man horseback riding, or cold baths, or walking barefoot. Asclepius was the Greek god of healing, and in Marcus's world people spoke of his prescriptions the way we speak of a doctor's orders. In the same way, he says, the nature of the whole prescribed for this person an illness, or a disability, or a loss. The word for prescribed is the same. In his view the event isn't random; it's fitted to you, the way a prescription is written for one patient. He gives two reasons to accept it. One: it happened to you, it was assigned to you, it's woven into your own life. Two: it serves the health of the whole universe, which he believed was one living order. You don't have to share his belief about the cosmos to feel the force of the first reason. This is your life, and this is in it. So, he says, accept what happens the way you accept what the doctor orders. Many prescriptions are bitter, and we welcome them anyway, hoping for health. You can't always choose whether hard things come. But you can choose their column: bad luck, to be resented, or medicine, to be taken. Marcus isn't saying it doesn't taste bitter. He's saying bitter isn't the same as wrong.
screen: `ASCLEPIUS PRESCRIBED A COLD BATH.` · `NATURE PRESCRIBED AN ILLNESS.` · `YOURS, AND PART OF THE WHOLE.` · `BITTER, BUT TAKEN FOR HEALTH.` · then, large: `THE PRESCRIPTION.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one hard thing in your life right now, an ache, a limit, a loss, a difficult person, and notice which column it's been in. Just for these breaths, picture it on a prescription pad with your name at the top, and ask Marcus's first question: is this part of my own life, assigned to me? Then take it, the way you'd take a bitter pill the doctor ordered.
Nature's prescription. Marcus says as a doctor prescribes cold baths, nature prescribes illness or loss: take it as medicine, bitter but meant for health. Today's word.
Your line: the prescription. Bitter isn't the same as wrong. Take good care.

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius sometimes reframe a hardship as in Meditations 5.8, accepting it as a doctor's order rather than resenting it only as bad luck.

notes: 5.8 paraphrased: as we say Asclepius prescribed horse exercise, cold baths, or going without shoes, so nature prescribed disease, mutilation, loss; two reasons to be content: it was done for you, prescribed and related to you, woven into your destiny; and it is a cause of the well-being and perfection of the whole; accept it as we accept what Asclepius prescribes, many things disagreeable but welcomed for the hope of health. Confirm. Marcus uses the same verb (suntasso) for both prescriptions: confirm.
Temple incubation at Asclepieia (e.g., Epidaurus, Pergamon): standard. Galen's devotion to Asclepius (he called himself the god's servant): confirm.
